title: Confined Riesz gas: From Newtonian Dynamics to Emergent Hydrodynamics
authors: Indranil Mukherjee, Abhishek Dhar, Manas Kulkarni
abstract: We investigate the real-time dynamics of the Riesz gas (RG), a paradigmatic system of particles with power-law interactions that encapsulates several many-body interacting classical systems. While the equilibrium properties of the system have been extensively studied the connection between microscopic dynamics, macroscopic evolution and thermalization has remained largely unexplored. Combining extensive large-scale Newtonian simulations with a hydrodynamic framework formulated in terms of three coarse grained fields -- density, velocity, and temperature -- we establish a direct and quantitative correspondence between the two descriptions. The hydrodynamic theory incorporates two phenomenological transport coefficients, the bulk viscosity $ξ$ and thermal conductivity $κ$, which encode dissipative effects at a macroscopic level. By analyzing representative classes of initial conditions, such as dome-like and Newton-cradle-type profiles, we find excellent agreement between microscopic and hydrodynamic evolution over a broad range of timescales, starting from relatively early all the way up to times at which steady state is attained. Notably, this agreement persists across a substantial window of $ξ$ and $κ$, demonstrating the robustness of the emergent hydrodynamic description. Our results provide a systematic validation of hydrodynamics in the RG and establish a concrete bridge between Newtonian dynamics and continuum theories in systems with power-law interactions, starting from first principles.
summary: This paper rigorously connects the microscopic, Newtonian dynamics of the Riesz gas to its macroscopic behavior using a hydrodynamic framework. By simulating the system from highly non-equilibrium states, the authors demonstrate that the evolution is quantitatively captured by continuum equations involving viscosity and thermal conductivity. This establishes a powerful theoretical bridge between particle-level interactions and continuum physics for systems with power-law forces.
main_problem: The study aims to establish a quantitative link between the real-time, microscopic dynamics of the Riesz gas (RG) governed by Newtonian mechanics and its macroscopic evolution described by a continuum hydrodynamic framework.
main_result: Excellent and robust agreement is found between the full time evolution from Newtonian simulations and the three-field hydrodynamic theory across various initial conditions and timescales.
method: The authors combine large-scale Newtonian molecular dynamics simulations with the derivation and numerical solution of coupled hydrodynamic equations incorporating bulk viscosity and thermal conductivity.
model_or_system: The system is the Riesz gas, characterized by particles interacting via power-law potentials and confined by a quadratic trap. The dynamics are analyzed by coarse-graining the system into fields for density, velocity, and temperature.
key_observables: Time evolution of density ($ho$), momentum ($\mathbf{p}$), and temperature ($T$) profiles.
important_parameters: Power-law exponent ($k$), interaction strength ($J$), trap frequency ($\omega$), and phenomenological transport coefficients ($\xi$ and $\kappa$).
main_assumptions: The hydrodynamic description relies on introducing phenomenological transport coefficients ($\xi$ and $\kappa$), and the comparison is most robust for parameters near specific reference values.
figures_summary: Figures compare the time evolution of $ho, \mathbf{p}, T$ for dome-like and Newton-cradle-type initial conditions, contrasting results from full simulations against the hydrodynamic model predictions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the microscopic Hamiltonian and simulating dynamics, then deriving the coarse-grained hydrodynamic equations, and finally performing a quantitative comparison of the time evolution and steady-state profiles between the two descriptions.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, first-principles validation of continuum hydrodynamics for a complex, interacting classical system with power-law interactions, bridging microscopic dynamics to macroscopic transport theory.
